units.text: QUANTUM GROUPS AND RIBBON G-CATEGORIES
Introduction

In order to construct 3-dimensional homotopy quantum field theories (HQFT's), the second author introduced for a group G the notions of a ribbon G-category and a modular (ribbon) G-category. The aim of this paper is to analyze the categories of representations of quantum groups (at roots of unity) from this prospective. The role of G will be played by the center of the corresponding Lie algebra.

We begin with a general theory of ribbon G-categories with abelian G. According to [Tu4], any modular (ribbon) G-category C gives rise to a 3-dimensional HQFT with target K(G, 1). Such an HQFT comprises several ingredients including a "homotopy modular functor" assigning modules to pairs (a surface Σ, an element of H 1 (Σ; G)) and a numerical invariant of pairs (a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a cohomology class ξ ∈ H 1 (M; G)). We introduce here a larger class of weakly non-degenerate premodular G-categories. Similarly to [Tu4], each such category C gives rise to a numerical invariant τ C (M, ξ) of pairs (M, ξ) as above. If C satisfies an additional assumption of regularity and G is finite then the standard Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant τ C (M) is also defined and splits as where b 1 (M) is the first Betti number of M. Note that the invariant τ C (M, ξ) extends to an HQFT provided C is a modular G-category.

Let g be a simple complex Lie algebra and ε be a complex root of unity. We show that under certain assumptions on the order of ε, the pair (g, ε) gives rise to a premodular ribbon G-category C = C(g, ε) where G is the center of g. (For the center groups of simple Lie algebras, see Table 1 below). The definition of C is based on a study of the representations of the quantum group U q (g), cf. [AP,Lu,Le2]. We specify conditions on ε which ensure that C is regular so that we have numerical invariants of 1-cohomology classes and a splitting of the standard WRT-invariant as above. Another set of conditions ensures that C is a modular G-category. The resulting 3-dimensional HQFT is however not very interesting since it splits as a product of a standard TQFT and a homological HQFT (cf. Remark 3.5).
The first author is partially supported by an NSF grant.

The paper consists of three sections. In Sect. 1 we discuss the theory of premodular Gcategories with abelian G. In Sect. 2 we recall the definition of τ C (M, ξ) and briefly discuss the homotopy modular functor. In Sect. 3 we consider the category C(g, ε).
The first author would like to thank A. Beliakova, C. Blanchet, A. Bruguieres, G. Masbaum for helpful discussions.
Premodular G-categories
Throughout this section, G denotes an abelian group and K a field of characteristic zero.

1.1. Preliminaries on monoidal categories. We shall use the standard notions of the theory of monoidal categories, see [Ma]. Recall that a left duality in a monoidal category C associates to any object V ∈ C an object V * ∈ C and two morphisms b V : 1 I → V ⊗V * and d V : V * ⊗V → 1 I satisfying the identities
(id V ⊗ d V ) (b V ⊗ id V ) = id V , (d V ⊗ id V * )(id V * ⊗ b V ) = id V * .

Here 1 I denotes the unit object of C and for simplicity we omit the associativity isomorphisms and the canonical isomorphisms 1 I ⊗ V ≈ V ≈ V ⊗ 1 I. An object of C isomorphic to 1 I is said to be trivial.
A monoidal category C is K-additive if all the Hom ′ s in C are K-modules and both the composition and the tensor product of morphisms are bilinear over K.
We say that a K-additive monoidal category C splits as a disjoint union of subcategories {C α } numerated by certain α if:
-each C α is a full subcategory of C; -each object of C belongs to C α for a unique α; -if V ∈ C α and W ∈ C β with α = β then Hom C (V, W ) = 0.
1.2. Ribbon G-categories. A monoidal G-category over K is a K-additive monoidal category with left duality C which splits as a disjoint union of subcategories
{C α } numerated by α ∈ G such that (i) if V ∈ C α and W ∈ C β then V ⊗ W ∈ C α+β ; (ii) if V ∈ C α then V * ∈ C −α .

We shall write C = ∐ α C α and call the subcategories {C α } of C the components of C. The category C 0 corresponding to the neutral element 0 ∈ G is called the neutral component of C. Conditions (i) and (ii) show that C 0 is closed under tensor multiplication and taking the dual object. Condition (i) implies that 1 I ∈ C 0 . Thus, C 0 is a monoidal category with left duality.
The standard notions of braidings and twists in monoidal categories apply in this setting without any changes. A braiding (resp. twist) in a monoidal G-category C is a system of invertible morphisms
{c V,W : V ⊗ W → W ⊗ V } V,W ∈C (resp. {θ V : V → V } V ∈C )

satisfying the usual conditions, see [KRT,Tu2]. We say that a monoidal G-category is ribbon if it is ribbon in the sense of [Tu2], i.e., if it has braiding and twist compatible with each other and with duality.

The standard theory of ribbon categories applies to any ribbon G-category C. Suppose that L is a framed oriented m-component link in S 3 whose components are ordered, and X 1 , . . . , X m are K-linear combinations of objects of C. Then there is defined the quantum Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant L(X 1 , . . . , X m ) ∈ End C (1 I). In particular, for any object X ∈ C, we have a dimension dim(X) = U(X) ∈ End C (1 I) where U is an oriented unknot with framing 0.
For any endomorphism f : X → X, we have a well-defined trace tr(f ) ∈ End C (1 I) so that tr(id X ) = dim(X).

1.3. Premodular G-categories. Let C be a ribbon G-category. An object V of C is simple if End C (V ) = K id V . It is clear that an object isomorphic or dual to a simple object is itself simple. The assumption that K is a field and [Tu2,Lemma II.4.2.3] imply that any non-zero morphism between simple objects is an isomorphism.

We say that an object V of C is dominated by simple objects if there is a finite set of simple objects {V r } r of C (possibly with repetitions) and morphisms {f r : V r → V, g r : V → V r } r such that id V = r f r g r . Clearly, if V ∈ C α then without loss of generality we can assume that V r ∈ C α for all r.
We say that a ribbon G-category C is premodular if it satisfies the following three axioms: (1.3.1) the unit object 1 I is simple;
(1.3.2) for each α ∈ G, the set I α of the isomorphism classes of simple objects of C α is finite;

(1.3.3) for each α ∈ G, any object of C α is dominated by simple objects of C α . According to [Tu4,Remark 7.8] the set G C = {α ∈ G | C α = ∅} is a subgroup of G. The theory certainly reduces to G C . For simplicity, we will assume from now on that G = G C .
Recall that U is an unknot with framing 0. Let U ± be an unknot with framing ±1. For each α ∈ G, consider the formal linear combination
ω α = i∈Iα dim(V i )V i where V i is a simple object in C α representing i ∈ I α . Define ∆ α = U(ω α ) = i∈Iα dim(V i ) 2 , ∆ ± α = U ± (ω α ) = i∈Iα v ±1 i dim(V i ) 2 ,

1.6. Modular G-categories. Let C be a premodular G-category. For i, j ∈ I = ∪ α∈G I α , choose simple objects V i , V j ∈ C representing i, j, respectively, and set
S i,j = H(V i , V j ) = tr(c V j ,V i • c V i ,V j : V i ⊗ V j → V i ⊗ V j ) ∈ End C (1 I) = K.
Here H is the standard Hopf link in S 3 with framing 0. It follows from the properties of the trace that S i,j does not depend on the choice of V i , V j in the isomorphism classes i, j.
A premodular G-category C is modular if the following axiom is satisfied.
(Non-degeneracy axiom) The (finite) square matrix [S i,j ] i,j∈I 0 is invertible over K.

It follows from this axiom that the neutral component C 0 of C is a modular ribbon category in the usual, ungraded sense (see [Tu2]). It is known that the non-degeneracy implies the weak non-degeneracy.

A modular ribbon G-category C may be non-modular in the ungraded sense because the set I = ∪ α∈G I α of the isomorphism classes of simple objects in C may be infinite, or because the full S-matrix [S i,j ] i,j∈I may be non-invertible.
Proposition 1.9. Suppose that G is finite and a modular G-category C is regular. Then C is a modular category in the ungraded sense.
Proof. According to [Br], [BB], a premodular category C is modular if and only if it has no nontrivial C-transparent simple objects and i∈I (dim

(V i )) 2 = 0. If V is a C-transparent simple object of C then V ∈ M C ⊂ C 0 . But since C 0 is modular, V is a trivial object. By Corollary 1.2, i∈I (dim(V i )) 2 = |G| ∆ 0 = 0, since C 0 is modular.

2. Invariants of 3-manifolds and HQFT's 2.1. Invariants of 3-dimensional G-manifolds. Fix an abelian group G. Let C be a weakly non-degenerate premodular ribbon G-category over a field of zero characteristic K. We explain here following [Tu4] that C gives rise to a topological invariant of 1-dimensional cohomology classes of 3-manifolds with coefficients in G.

Fix an element D ∈ K such that D 2 = ∆ 0 . Let M be a closed connected oriented 3dimensional manifold and ξ ∈ H 1 (M; G). Present M as the result of surgery on S 3 along a framed oriented link L = L 1 ∪ ... ∪ L m . Recall that M is obtained by gluing m solid tori to the exterior of L in S 3 . This allows us to consider for n = 1, ..., m, the value, α n ∈ G, of ξ on the meridian of L n and provide L n with the color ω αn = i∈Iα n dim(V i )V i . Let σ + (resp. σ − ) be the number of positive (resp. negative) squares in the diagonal decomposition of the intersection form H 2 (W L ) × H 2 (W L ) → Z where W L is the compact oriented 4-manifold bounded by M and obtained from the 4-ball B 4 by attaching 2-handles along tubular neighborhoods of the components of L in S 3 = ∂B 4 . Set
τ C,D (M, ξ) = D −b 1 (M )−1 (∆ − 0 ) −σ − (∆ + 0 ) −σ + L(ω α 1 , . . . , ω αm ) ∈ K, where b 1 (M) = m − σ + − σ − is the first Betti number of M.

It follows from [Tu4,Theorem 7.3] that τ C,D (M, ξ) is a homeomorphism invariant of the pair (M, ξ) (in [Tu4] this is stated for modular G-categories, but the proof remains true for weakly non-degenerate premodular categories). The factor D −b 1 (M )−1 appears here for normalization purposes.

As in the standard theory, the invariant τ C,D (M, ξ) generalizes to an invariant of triples (M, Ω, ξ) where M is as above, Ω is a colored ribbon graph in M and ξ ∈ H 1 (M\Ω; G). Here a coloring is understood as the usual coloring of Ω over C such that the color of every 1-stratum t of Ω is an object in C α(t) where α(t) ∈ G is the value of ξ on the meridian of t. This notion of a coloring applies in particular to framed oriented links in M so that we obtain an isotopy invariant of triples (M, L, ξ) where M is as above, L is a colored framed oriented link in M and ξ ∈ H 1 (M\L; G).
Suppose now that G is finite and C is regular. Set ω = α∈G ω α . By Lemma 1.8, Proof. The proof in [Bl,section 5] can be applied to get the result.

2.1. The homotopy modular functor. A modular G-category C (not necessarily regular) gives rise to a 3-dimensional HQFT, see [Tu4]. In particular, the homotopy modular functor T C associated with C assigns K-modules to so-called extended G-surfaces and assigns K-linear isomorphisms of these modules to weak homeomorphisms of such surfaces. We recall here the definition of an extended G-surface and the corresponding K-module in our abelian case.

Let Υ be a closed oriented surface. A point p ∈ Υ is marked if is equipped with a sign ε p = ±1 and a tangent direction, i.e., a ray R + v where v is a non-zero tangent vector at p. A marking of Υ is a finite (possibly void) set of distinct marked points P ⊂ Υ. A G-marking of Υ is a marking P ⊂ Υ endowed with a cohomology class ξ ∈ H 1 (Υ\P ; G). A G-marking P ⊂ Υ is colored if it is equipped with a function x which assigns to every point p ∈ P an object x p ∈ C ξ(µp) where µ p is a small loop in Υ\P encircling p in the direction induced by the orientation of Υ if ε p = +1 and in the opposite direction otherwise.

An extended G-surface comprises a closed oriented surface Υ, a colored G-marking P ⊂ Υ, and a Lagrangian space λ ⊂ H 1 (Υ; R). The corresponding K-module is defined as follows. Assume that Υ is a connected surface of genus n and P = {p 1 , ..., p m } ⊂ Υ. For r = 1, ..., m, set ε r = ε pr = ±1, µ r = µ pr and x r = x pr ∈ C. The group π 1 (Υ\P ) is generated by the homotopy classes of loops µ ′ 1 , ..., µ ′ m homotopic to µ 1 , ..., µ m , respectively, and by 2n elements a 1 , b 1 , ..., a n , b n subject to the only relation

(µ ′ 1 ) ε 1 ... (µ ′ m ) εm [a 1 , b 1 ] ... [a n , b n ] = 1 where [a, b] = aba −1 b −1 . Then T C (Υ, P, ξ, x, λ) = i 1 ∈I ξ(a 1 ) ,=2E..,in∈I ξ(an) Hom C 1 I, (x 1 ) ε 1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ (x m ) εm ⊗ n s=1 V is ⊗ V * is

where for an object x ∈ C we set x 1 = x and x −1 = x * . Observe that the dimension of T (Υ, P, ξ, x, λ) over K does not depend on the values of ξ on b 1 , ..., b n . This implies that this dimension does not depend on the choice of ξ. For ξ = 0, this dimension is computed by the Verlinde formula. In particular, if P = ∅ we obtain Dim T C (Υ, P, ξ, x, λ) = Dim T C (Υ, P, 0, x, λ) = D 2n−2 i∈I 0 (dim(V i )) 2−2n .
The same formula can be deduced from the generalised Verlinde formula for HQFT's given in [Tu3,Sect. 4.11].

Remark 2.2. Since we restrict ourselves here to abelian G, the homotopy classes of maps from a manifold M to the Eilenberg-MacLane space K(G, 1) are classified by elements of H 1 (M; G). This allows one to formulate HQFT's with target K(G, 1) in terms of 1-dimensional cohomology classes. We call the HQFT's arising from modular G-categories with abelian G and trivial crossed structure (as everywhere in this paper) abelian. The abelian HQFT's are simpler than the general HQFT's. One of simplifications is that in the abelian case we can forget about base points (in the general case one has to work in the pointed category). Also, in the abelian case the canonical action of G on the spaces of conformal blocks T (Υ, P, ξ, x, λ) defined in [Tu4,Sect. 10.3] is trivial.

3. Premodular G-categories derived from quantum groups 3.1. Fusion category associated with quantum groups at roots of unity. We will briefly recall the fusion categories of quantum groups at roots of unity, mainly to fix notation. We refer the reader to [AP, GK, Ki] for details. Let g be a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over C. Fix a Cartan subalgebra and a system of basis roots α 1 , . . . , α ℓ . Choose the inner product on h * = R-span α 1 , . . . , α ℓ such that the square length of any short root is 2. Let G = X/Y be the quotient of the weight lattice X by the root lattice Y . It is known that G is isomorphic to the center of the simply-connected Lie group associated with g, and |G| is equal to the determinant of the Cartan matrix. Let d be the maximal absolute value of the non-diagonal entries of the Cartan matrix. Let h denote the Coxeter number of g and h ∨ the dual Coxeter number of g. By D we denote the smallest positive integer such that D(x|y) ∈ Z for all x, y ∈ X. The data associated with simple Lie algebras is given in Table 1.

The quantum group U v (g), as defined in [AP, Lu], is a Hopf algebra over Q(v), with v a formal variable. There is an integral version of U v (g), defined over the ring Z[v, v −1 ], introduced by Lusztig. For ε ∈ C, let U ε (g) be the Hopf algebra over C obtained by tensoring the integral version of U v (g) with C, where C is considered as a Z[v, v −1 ]-module by v → ε (see [AP, Lu]).

Let ε be a root of unity. The fusion categoryC(g, ε) is the quotient of the category of all tilting U ε (g)-modules by negligible modules and negligible morphisms (see [AP], thereC(g, ε) is denoted by C − ). The categoryC(g, ε) is a semisimple monoidal C-abelian category with duality. The isomorphism classes of simple objects inC(g, ε) are parametrized by the dominant weights µ such that µ + ρ ∈ C ε where ρ is the half-sum of all positive roots and C ε is defined as follows. There are two cases depending on the order r of the root of unity ε 2 .
Case 1: The numbers r and d are co-prime and r > h. Then
C ε = {x ∈ C | (x|α 0 ) < r}
where C is the Weyl chamber and α 0 is the short highest root, i.e., the only root in C with square length 2.
Case 2: r is divisible by d and r/d > h ∨ . Then
C ε = {x ∈ C | (x|β 0 ) < r}

where β 0 is the long highest root, i.e., the only root in C with square length 2d. Note that when d = 1, the two cases overlap and the definitions of C ε agree. In [Le1], C ε is denoted by C ′ r . For a dominant weight µ such that µ + ρ ∈ C ε there is a simple U ε (g)-module Λ µ ∈C(g, ε), known as the Weyl module, which is a deformation of the corresponding classical g-module.

It represents the isomorphism class numerated by µ. The decomposition of a tensor product Λ µ ⊗ Λ ν is described in [AP] (the tensor product is denoted there by ⊗, but we will use the usual notation). For our purposes, we notice that if Λ γ appears as a summand in Λ µ ⊗ Λ ν , then µ + ν − w · γ ∈ Y for some w ∈ W ε where W ε is the group of affine transformations of h * generated by the reflections in the walls of the simplexC ε , the topological closure of C ε , and the dot action is the one shifted by ρ so that w · x = w(x + ρ) − ρ. Note thatC ε is a fundamental domain of W ε . For further use, we state here a simple lemma.
Lemma 3.1. For every x ∈ X and w ∈ W ε , one has x − w · x ∈ Y .

Proof. It is known that W ε = W ⋉ Q, where W is the usual Weyl group, and Q is the Z-lattice spanned by the long roots. (One considers Q as a group of translations). Obviously, Q ⊂ Y . If w ∈ Q, the statement is trivial. If w ∈ W , the statement is well-known in the theory of simple Lie algebras.

3.2. Braiding and twist inC(g, ε). There are a braiding and a twist inC(g, ε) which makẽ C(g, ε) a ribbon category. They depend on a choice of a complex root of unity ζ such that ζ D = ε, where D is as in Table 1. Let us denote the resulting ribbon category byC(g, ε; ζ). The tensor structure inC(g, ε; ζ) and the corresponding Verlinde algebra do not depend on the choice of ζ.

The ribbon categoryC(g, ε; ζ) is premodular, since it has only a finite number of isomorphism classes of simple objects. It is also Hermitian, see [Ki], so that dim(V ) ∈ R for every V ∈ C(g, ε; ζ). (This can also be deduced from the explicit formulas for the quantum dimensions of the Weyl modules). Thus for every simple object x, one has (dimx) 2 is a positive real number (since dim(x) = 0).

In Case 2 if ε = e πi/r , then this Hermitian structure is known to be unitary, see [We]. Then dim(V ) > 0 for every V ∈C(g, ε; ζ). Again this can also be deduced from the explicit formulas for the quantum dimensions of the Weyl modules.

It is clear that ζ 2Dr = 1 where r is the order of ε 2 . When r is divisible by d, r/d > h ∨ , and ζ has order 2Dr, the categoryC(g, ε; ζ) is modular. These are the well-known, and so far the main, examples of modular category.

3.3.C(g, ε; ζ) as a premodular G-category. Let π : X → G = X/Y be the projection. For α ∈ G, let I α be the set of dominant weights µ such that µ + ρ ∈ C ε and π(µ) = α. Let C α = C α (g, ε; ζ) be the set of all objects inC(g, ε; ζ) which are direct sums of Λ µ with µ ∈ I α . Set C = ⊔ α∈G C α . We consider C as a full subcategory ofC(g, ε; ζ).
Proposition 3.2. The category C = ⊔ α∈G C α is a premodular G-category.
Proof. One only needs to check (i) and (ii) of Sect. 1.2.
(i) Let µ ∈ I α , ν ∈ I β , and Λ λ be a direct summand of Λ µ ⊗ Λ ν . Then µ + ν − w · λ ∈ Y for some w ∈ W ε . Lemma 3.1 shows that π(λ) = π(µ) + π(ν), or, in other words, λ ∈ I α+β .
(ii) The dual of Λ µ is Λ −w 0 (µ) , where w 0 is the longest element of the Weyl group. Again Lemma 3.1 shows that −w 0 (µ) ∈ I −α .

If all the colors of a framed link L are simple g-modules with highest weights in the root lattice, then the quantum invariant of L is in Z[v 2 , v −2 ], according to the integrality, see [Le1]. Hence the fact that C is a modular, or weakly non-degenerate, G-category does not depend on the choice of the D-th root ζ of ε; it totally depends on the order r of ε 2 . Note that the fact C(g, ε; ζ) is a (non-graded) modular category does depend on the choice of ζ.

3.4. Modular G-categories. The following proposition shows that in Case 1 of Sect. 3.1, the category C constructed above is a modular G-category, at least under the assumption that r is co-prime with |G|.
Proposition 3.3. Suppose that the order r of ε 2 is co-prime with d |G| and r > h. Then C is a modular G-category.
Proof. We need only to prove that the S-matrix of the neutral component C 0 is invertible. This was established in [Le2,Theorem 3.3].
The following proposition shows that C can be G-modular even when r is not co-prime with d|G|.

Proposition 3.4. Suppose g is a Lie algebra of series C ℓ with odd ℓ. Assume that the order r of ε 2 is even but not divisible by 4 and r > dh ∨ . Then C is a modular G-category. (Note that for C ℓ , one has d = 2, D = 1, and h ∨ = ℓ + 1.) A proof will be given later.

Remark 3.5. In the cases of Propositions 3.3 and 3.4, it can be shown that the category C is the product of its neutral component and a modular category associated with the center group G (see the definition in [Sa], see also [Le2]). The corresponding invariant of a 1-cohomology class on a 3-manifold M is then the product of the invariant of the cohomology class 0 with an invariant depending only on H 1 (M; Z) and the linking form. The theory in this case is rather trivial.

3.5. Regularity of C. In Case 2 of Sect. 3.1, the premodular G-category C constructed above turns out to be regular, at least under a few further assumptions on ζ and r. where ℓ is the rank of g, and a . . .b means a is divisible by b. Then the premodular G-category C is regular.
When g = sl n , the condition on r can be rephrased as r > n and (r − n)(n − 1) is divisible by 2n. Thus we recover the sl 2 -case of [KM,Tu1] and the sl n -case of [Mu, Bl].

Remark 3.7. One may ask when the G-category C is weakly-nondegenerate.
